newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon seen reviving its own '70s style.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon seen reviving its own '70s style.

text.p: After swallowing GM's Hughes Aircraft business, the new Raytheon Corp will look a lot like the defense specialist it was in the 1970s, analysts said on Thursday.

"It is clear that the end of the Cold War, and the resulting decline in the U.S. defense procurement budget, have brought about fundamental changes to the defense industry requiring continued consolidation," said Dennis J. Picard, Raytheon's chairman and chief executive officer, in announcing the $9.5 billion deal with General Motors Co.

Those changes have led Lexington, Mass.-based Raytheon to move away from its previous strategy of buying companies to diversify and insulate itself from U.S. Defense Department cuts. It no longer seems to be placing an emphasis on being "a diversified commericial company," as the company's annual reports have trumpeted, analysts said.

"It will be a majority defense electronics company," Edward Jones analyst William Fiala said. "And I would venture to say that it will look to spin off or outright sell one of three businesses - appliances, aircraft and or Engineering and Construction."

Under the agreement, Raytheon will acquire $4.4 billion of Hughes debt. The company is expected to sell off some divisions or transfer some of that debt to a spin-off. It will finance the remainder of the Hughes transaction with a $5.1 billion stock swap.

Fourteen Research analyst Anthony Ginsberg said Raytheon's previous strategy of buying companies outside of defense once made sense. "But if you look at it from today's perspective in the defense industry, a flaw was revealed," he said. "None of the companies they invested in is number one in their field."
But Ginsberg said, "Amana should be easy to sell," naming Maytag Corp as a likely buyer.
Analsyts said another source of capital could be Raytheon's $3 billion Engineering and Constructors (E&C) division. Raytheon's CEO Dennis Picard has called E&C a "trapped asset."
"E&C's main competitors right now would be Fluor Corp and Foster Wheeler Corp, and their (price earnings ratios) are much higher than Raytheon's as a whole," Fiala said.
On Thursday, Clinton, N.J.-based Foster Wheeler was trading at $39 a share, with a p/e ratio of 37.03. Irvine, Calif.-based Fluor was trading at 68-3/4, with a p/e ratio of 21.33.

Raytheon was trading at 48-1/2, with a p/e ratio of 13.6 in late trading. The ratio represents the current market price of a company's stock expressed as multiple of its earnings per share for the previous 12 months.

"I can see them spinning off E&C or selling it," Fiala said. "As a spin-off they can allocate debt to it, and it's a tax-free deal. As a sale, they'll have to pay taxes, so it depends on the bids they would get."
Ginsburg said he expected Raytheon's share price to go down on a short-term basis, but divesting "these other assets could provide better support for the stock price."
